introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER the a, b and c OR the d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is recorded data from an experiment to investigate the relationship between acceleration, a, and force, F.

| F / N | 0 | 14 | 30 | 45 | 61 | 75 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a / m s$^{-2}$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

(i) Define acceleration. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Plot a graph of force, F, on the Y-axis against acceleration, a, on the X-axis. *[6 marks]*

(iii) Determine the slope of the graph. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** **Acceleration** is the **rate of change of velocity**, that is, the change in velocity per unit time: $a = \dfrac{v-u}{t}$. Its unit is $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

**(ii)** Graph to draw:

- **Axes:** $a/\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ on the X-axis from $0$ to $5$ (for example $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$); $F/\mathrm{N}$ on the Y-axis from $0$ to $80$ (for example $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $5\,\mathrm{N}$). Both axes labelled with their units, scales uniform, using more than half of the sheet.
- **Points to plot:** $(0, 0)$, $(1, 14)$, $(2, 30)$, $(3, 45)$, $(4, 61)$, $(5, 75)$, each marked with a small neat cross.
- **Line:** the points lie very close to a **straight line through the origin** ($F = 0$ when $a = 0$). Draw one straight line of best fit with a ruler, with the points evenly scattered on both sides of it (the points $(1, 14)$ and $(4, 61)$ are slightly off the line because of experimental error). The graph shows that $F$ is **directly proportional** to $a$.

**(iii)** The slope is $\dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta a}$, read from a large triangle on the line, using two points far apart, for example $(0, 0)$ and $(5, 75)$:

$$\text{slope} = \frac{75 - 0}{5 - 0}\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}} = 15\,\mathrm{N\,s^{2}\,m^{-1}} = 15\,\mathrm{kg}$$

**The slope is about $15\,\mathrm{kg}$** (accept $14$ to $16$). It is the **mass** of the object, because $F = ma$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 4 shows a uniform metre rule (of length $100\,\mathrm{cm}$) pivoted at the $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark and in equilibrium.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2025-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_8_fig_1.png)

*Figure 4*

(i) Calculate the weight of the metre rule. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the value of the reaction force, R, at the pivot on the metre rule. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The rule is in equilibrium, so by the **principle of moments** the clockwise moment about the pivot equals the anticlockwise moment.

- The $5\,\mathrm{N}$ load is $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the left of the pivot: anticlockwise moment $= 5 \times 30 = 150\,\mathrm{N\,cm}$.
- The weight $W$ of the uniform rule acts at its centre ($50\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark), which is $50 - 30 = 20\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the right of the pivot: clockwise moment $= W \times 20$.

$$W \times 20 = 5 \times 30 \quad\Rightarrow\quad W = \frac{150}{20} = 7.5\,\mathrm{N}$$

**The weight of the rule is $7.5\,\mathrm{N}$.**

**(ii)** For equilibrium the upward force equals the total downward force:

$$R = 5\,\mathrm{N} + W = 5 + 7.5 = 12.5\,\mathrm{N}$$

**The reaction at the pivot is $12.5\,\mathrm{N}$** (upwards).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State Newton's first law of motion. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Give one practical application of Newton's first law of motion. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** **Newton's first law:** a body remains at rest, or continues to move with **uniform velocity in a straight line**, unless it is acted upon by a **resultant external force**.

**(ii)** Any one of: **seat belts** in a car (when the car stops suddenly the passengers tend to keep moving forward, the belt stops them); passengers in a bus are thrown forward when it brakes suddenly; a coin on a card stays in place when the card is flicked away; head restraints on car seats.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is recorded data from an experiment to investigate the relationship between the resistance, R, of a material and its length, l.

| l / m | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R / $\Omega$ | 12 | 23 | 30 | 46 | 58 | 70 |

(i) Define resistance. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Plot a graph of resistance, R, on the Y-axis against length, l, on the X-axis. *[6 marks]*

(iii) Determine the slope of the graph. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **resistance** of a conductor is the **ratio of the potential difference across it to the current flowing through it**: $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$. It measures the opposition of the conductor to the flow of current; its unit is the **ohm ($\Omega$)**.

**(ii)** Graph to draw:

- **Axes:** $l/\mathrm{m}$ on the X-axis from $0$ to $12$ (for example $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $1\,\mathrm{m}$); $R/\Omega$ on the Y-axis from $0$ to $80$ (for example $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $10\,\Omega$). Both axes labelled with units, uniform scales.
- **Points to plot:** $(2, 12)$, $(4, 23)$, $(6, 30)$, $(8, 46)$, $(10, 58)$, $(12, 70)$.
- **Line:** five of the points lie close to a straight line through the origin; the point $(6, 30)$ lies well below it (about $35\,\Omega$ would be expected) and is an **anomalous point**, probably a reading error, which is ignored when drawing the line. Draw one straight line of best fit through the origin and the five other points. The graph shows that $R$ is **directly proportional** to $l$.

**(iii)** Slope $= \dfrac{\Delta R}{\Delta l}$ from a large triangle on the line, for example between $(2, 11.6)$ and $(12, 69.6)$ read on the line:

$$\text{slope} = \frac{69.6 - 11.6}{12 - 2} = \frac{58}{10} = 5.8\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$$

**The slope is about $5.8\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$** (accept $5.7$ to $5.9$). It is the **resistance per metre of the material**, equal to $\rho / A$ (resistivity divided by cross-sectional area).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 shows a modern socket used for house wiring.

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2025-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_8_fig_2.png)

*Figure 5*

(i) Name the wires represented by the letters X, Y and Z. *[3 marks]*

(ii) If the mains voltage is $220\,\mathrm{V}$ and a device in the house has a resistance of $100\,\Omega$, calculate the current flowing through the device. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

- **X** is the **live wire** (it carries the fuse, which must be in the live wire so that the appliance is cut off from the mains when the fuse blows).
- **Y** is the **neutral wire** (completes the circuit).
- **Z** is the **earth wire** (joined to the metal case of the appliance, as a safety connection).

**(ii)**

$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{220\,\mathrm{V}}{100\,\Omega} = 2.2\,\mathrm{A}$$

**The current through the device is $2.2\,\mathrm{A}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State Ohm's law. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Give an example of an Ohmic conductor. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** **Ohm's law:** the current flowing through a conductor is **directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends**, provided the **temperature and other physical conditions stay constant** ($V \propto I$, or $V/I = $ constant).

**(ii)** A **metallic wire** (for example copper, nichrome or constantan) kept at constant temperature, or a fixed carbon or wire-wound resistor.
